spans.text: Knowledge work is slow mostly because it waits, not because people work slowly.
Queueing arithmetic makes waiting grow in proportion to work in progress and explode once utilization passes about 80%.
So the lever is limiting work in progress and keeping slack, not pushing people harder.

items.text: Little's law.

Average work in progress equals throughput times time in the system, so more WIP at the same throughput means proportionally longer waits; the author returns to it in the chapters on WIP limits and batch size.
The utilization curve.
Waiting stays modest to about 70% utilization and then rises steeply, roughly nine times the service time at 90%.
Variability multiplies waiting.
Unpredictable arrivals and uneven work add to utilization's effect, which is why the same load feels fine one week and jammed the next.
WIP limits shorten cycle time.
In the author's twelve-week comparison, limits cut average cycle time from 31 to about 10 days while throughput stayed flat.
Small batches.
Smaller batches cut waiting for the same reason WIP limits do: less work sits in the system at once.
Hidden queues.
Most waiting happens in places nobody measures — approvals, hand-offs, work turned away at a limit — so it must be made visible before it can be managed.
Premise: delivery time is mostly waiting time.
Mechanism: Little's law and the utilization curve explain why waiting grows with load and variability.
Evidence: team data on WIP limits and batch sizes shows cycle time falling without lost throughput.
Implication: manage the flow of work, not the busyness of people.
Forecast delivery from work in progress divided by throughput instead of from effort estimates.
Set an explicit WIP limit and stop starting before you start finishing.
Plan with 15–20% of capacity unallocated.

spans.text: Responding to slow delivery by starting more work.

sections.title: Where it is weak or dated

items.text: The WIP-limit evidence comes from teams the author worked with, over twelve weeks; the case rests on a small, self-selected sample.
The formulas assume a single stable server; the author concedes they overstate waiting at low load and says little about teams where people share work.

reason.text: Treats the queue as a stock and a WIP limit as a balancing loop — the structural view behind this book's flow arithmetic.
